articles.title: Your Mac has been keeping a file on your family
articles.excerpt: Your Mac has been keeping a file on your family Since macOS 13 shipped in 2022, every Mac has run two daemons whose only job is to build a graph about you. Who you are, who you know, how those people…
articles.body: Your Mac has been keeping a file on your family Since macOS 13 shipped in 2022, every Mac has run two daemons whose only job is to build a graph about you. Who you are, who you know, how those people relate to you and to each other, how you communicate, where you go, what you do and when. The daemons are called knowledgeconstructiond and intelligenceplatformd, and the closest thing Apple has ever documented about them is a two-sentence man page. A security duo going by The Bishop and The Knight took the system apart in October and published the anatomy. The graph lives in ~/Library/IntelligencePlatform, fifty-one plaintext SQLite databases protected by macOS's Full Disk Access permission.
articles.author: ming ming

articles.title: Agent instructions: in the repo or in the tool?
articles.excerpt: There are two places to put the standing rules you want a coding agent to follow: in a file in the repo, or built into the tool that runs the agent. I've ended up with both, and they trade off differe…
articles.body: There are two places to put the standing rules you want a coding agent to follow: in a file in the repo, or built into the tool that runs the agent. I've ended up with both, and they trade off differently. In the repo, the rules are versioned. They show up in pull requests, the whole team sees them, and they travel with a clone. The cost is that you write and maintain them per project, and they're only as good as the last person who edited them. In the tool, they work in every project and for every agent with no setup. The cost is that they're invisible: nobody reviews a diff of them, and they can clash with how a particular repo does things. Styx does the second kind.
articles.author: Nic Flemmer

articles.title: Pydio Cells access needs a PAT, workspace, and public-share inventory
articles.excerpt: Pydio Cells access needs a PAT, workspace, and public-share inventory Pydio Cells combines identity, file storage, workspaces, OAuth clients, and public sharing. A person who reaches the login page ma…
articles.body: Pydio Cells access needs a PAT, workspace, and public-share inventory Pydio Cells combines identity, file storage, workspaces, OAuth clients, and public sharing. A person who reaches the login page may be blocked before seeing any files, while a leaked personal access token or public link may bypass the browser flow entirely. An exposure assessment that only records the login page leaves the important paths out. On 2026-11-08, ZoomEye count-only observations returned 0 matches for app="Pydio Cells" , 1,470 for title="Pydio Cells" , and 2,397 for http.body="Pydio Cells" . The query scope was sub_type=all , page 1, and page size 1. The title and body counts are close enough to be useful leads, but neither proves that a host is configured with public shares or weak tokens.

articles.body: Every few months someone asks "how long does Chrome Web Store review take now?" and the answers range from "two hours" to "three weeks". Both are true, because review time is not one number — it depends on what changed in the package. I keep timestamps for every submission of my extensions, so here is the real spread. The short version What you submitted Observed time Rejection (policy violation in the listing text) ~10 minutes Update, same permissions, small feature set same day – 1 day Update that adds a permission several days First submission of a new extension days to weeks The pattern is boring and consistent: review time tracks the permission delta, not the amount of code.

articles.title: Métodos HTTP: entendendo GET, POST, PUT, PATCH e DELETE
articles.excerpt: Imagine que estamos desenvolvendo uma API para gerenciar usuários. Precisamos consultar os usuários cadastrados, criar novos registros, atualizar informações e excluir aqueles que não são mais necessá…
articles.body: Imagine que estamos desenvolvendo uma API para gerenciar usuários. Precisamos consultar os usuários cadastrados, criar novos registros, atualizar informações e excluir aqueles que não são mais necessários. Todas essas operações podem acontecer por meio de requisições HTTP. Mas existe uma questão: como o servidor sabe o que queremos fazer com determinado recurso? É aí que entram os métodos HTTP. O que são métodos HTTP? Os métodos HTTP indicam a intenção de uma requisição. Eles comunicam ao servidor qual operação o cliente deseja realizar sobre um determinado recurso. Podemos fazer uma analogia com uma biblioteca. Imagine que você chega até o balcão e pode solicitar diferentes ações: consultar um livro, cadastrar um novo exemplar, atualizar informações do catálogo ou remover um registro.

articles.excerpt: Droynis keeps me accountable for the security settings I select.
articles.body: Part of the beauty of Android is its openness. It’s one of the many reasons why I would rather snag a Pixel or Galaxy device ahead of an iPhone. I can choose which default apps to employ, where I get them from, how I set up my phone, and even circumvent some restrictions if I’m feeling particularly spicy. A shortcoming of this borderless design is that Android users can often inadvertently set up an environment with potential security issues. As is so often the case with Android, that particular problem also breeds opportunity, and a new open-source app has jumped in to help Google solve it. It’s called Droynis , and it’s the security auditing tool that should’ve been a part of Android all along.

As Critical Role , the multimedia entertainment company Mercer co-founded, has grown and evolved over the years, one thing has remained constant: Mercer’s willingness to help other tabletop players. He is especially eager to support aspiring Dungeon Masters who hope to develop their skills and become as accomplished as he is, even appearing on the official Dungeons & Dragons YouTube page to provide assistance.

articles.title: Scientists simulate an Earth without life to help hunt for aliens and inhabited worlds
articles.excerpt: By modeling how a planet without life develops its atmosphere, astronomers hope to be able to better distinguish rocky planets without life from those that are inhabited.
articles.body: A new computer simulation that depicts Earth, or a rocky planet in general, without life is the latest tool in the quest to discover whether or not we are alone in the universe. Life leaves its mark on a planet, particularly its atmosphere, in the form of a mixture of biochemically created gases. Some are obvious, while others can be produced by both biology and geology, meaning that distinguishing a planet that has life from one that does not, solely based on what gases we can detect in its atmosphere, can be difficult. The key is in knowing which atmospheric conditions can be explained without life.

articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now. This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life. I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security. articles.body: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. | Photo: Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images Anthropic is using AI to build more powerful AI. And it appears to be working remarkably well, with the company's models improving roughly twice as quickly as a year ago, with little indication of slowing down. That's according to a new report published Thursday by the AI safety research organization METR, following an 11-week investigation inside the company, as part of a report evaluating its AI research and development. The probe is separate from a program offering safety researchers "employee-like" access to systems in the wake of high-profile hacking incidents over the summer.
